title: Mohammad Yousuf Says Pakistan Cricket's Decline Began After 2021 Win Over India
excerpt: The former batting great traced the national team's current crisis to the overconfidence that followed their famous T20 World Cup victory, while separately criticizing the PCB's mid-tour mass sacking during the England series.
body:
• Former Pakistan batter Mohammad Yousuf says the team's 10-wicket win over India at the 2021 T20 World Cup created a false sense of achievement that triggered the current decline
  • Yousuf pointed to ego, internal captaincy battles, and a lack of humility as the root causes of Pakistan cricket's sustained slump
  • The PCB sent home seven players and two coaches during the ongoing England Test tour after back-to-back heavy defeats gave England an unassailable 2-0 lead
  • Yousuf criticized the mid-tour overhaul as reflecting a "familiar cycle of internal chaos" rather than being purely performance-driven

Former Pakistan star cricketer Mohammad Yousuf has offered a striking diagnosis of the national team's extended slump, tracing its origins to an unlikely source: the famous 10-wicket victory over India at the 2021 T20 World Cup in Dubai.

Pakistan had never beaten India in a World Cup before that match. Babar Azam scored an unbeaten 68 while Mohammad Rizwan made 79 not out as Pakistan chased down 152 without losing a wicket. The win was celebrated as a historic moment — but Yousuf believes it was also a turning point in the wrong direction.

The Victory That Changed Everything

"That match which we won against India in 2021, that damaged us a lot. Because after that victory, players started to think that they had achieved something big. They couldn't understand what they had to do next."

https://x.com/MyAnandaBazar/status/2096600263981519272 — Mohammad Yousuf, speaking on Samaa TV

Instead of citing technical shortcomings or fitness issues, the former middle-order maestro singled out ego and a lack of humility as the primary drivers of Pakistan's downfall. He observed that players began acting as though they had reached the pinnacle of the sport, losing the grounded mentality required to sustain performance at the highest level.

"When you are performing well, you should stay humble. If you behave with your collar raised, and get disrespectful, problems will arrive. And a lot of them have arrived in Pakistan cricket," Yousuf said. "Everyone in the team was trying to become the captain of the Pakistan team. The consequences are still hurting Pakistan cricket."

A Pattern of Instability

Yousuf's comments carry additional weight given the backdrop of the current England tour, where the Pakistan Cricket Board made a dramatic overhaul of its Test squad. After the team slipped to an unassailable 0-2 deficit — losing the opening Test at Headingley by an innings and 103 runs, and the second at Lord's by 194 runs — the PCB sent home seven players and two members of the coaching staff ahead of the third Test at Edgbaston.

Mohammad Rizwan, Imam-ul-Haq, Salman Ali Agha, Ali Usman, Aamir Jamal, Muhammad Awais Zafar, and Khurram Shahzad were all released from the touring party. Head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and bowling coach Umar Gul were also removed, with white-ball head coach Mike Hesson and Ashley Noffke stepping in for the final Test, which starts September 9.

The PCB also issued a show-cause notice to the four-member national selection committee, demanding a written explanation within 24 hours on the reasoning behind player selections.

'This Is Not About Performance'

Yousuf argued that the scale of the mid-tour removals went beyond any straightforward performance rationale. The replacements arriving in England include five uncapped players, with a combined Test experience of just 10 matches across the entire incoming group.

"The recent decision by the authorities to recall players and coaching staff from the ongoing tour does not appear to be only performance related. After all, we are not sending legends like Zaheer Abbas, Javed Miandad, Inzamam-ul-Haq, or Saeed Anwar as replacements."

— Mohammad Yousuf, on X (formerly Twitter)

The former captain, who played 90 Tests and scored more than 7,500 runs for Pakistan, said the pattern of instability has repeated itself since the team's historic 1992 World Cup triumph. "Since the glory of the 1992 World Cup, such turbulence has resurfaced time and again, eroding stability and distracting from the game itself," he wrote.

Yousuf drew a sharp contrast between the current generation and his own era, noting that senior players like Saeed Anwar and Inzamam-ul-Haq always listened to coaches and respected team hierarchy. "Pakistan players after beating India in 2021 started thinking that they are the best and no one is better than them. They became disrespectful. If your head coach is talking, you are supposed to listen to him," he said.

His verdict reflects a growing consensus among Pakistan cricket observers: the team must embrace structural reform and fresh talent while rooting out the boardroom interference that has destabilized it for decades. Whether the overhauled squad can salvage any pride from the Edgbaston Test remains to be seen, but Yousuf's message is clear — the problems run far deeper than any single series result.
